abstract: We introduce the Segment Anything (SA) project: a new task, model, and dataset for image segmentation. Using our efficient model in a data collection loop, we built the largest segmentation dataset to date (by far), with over 1 billion masks on 11M licensed and privacy respecting images. The model is designed and trained to be promptable, so it can transfer zero-shot to new image distributions and tasks. We evaluate its capabilities on numerous tasks and find that its zero-shot performance is impressive – often competitive with or even superior to prior fully supervised results. We are releasing the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and corresponding dataset (SA-1B) of 1B masks and 11M images at https://segment-anything.com to foster research into foundation models for computer vision.

sections.body: The paper proposes a promptable segmentation task, the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and a data engine used to build SA-1B. SAM has an image encoder, a prompt encoder, and a mask decoder. Given an image embedding, the prompt encoder and mask decoder predict a mask from a prompt in about 50ms in a web browser. The data engine iterates between model-assisted annotation and retraining across three stages. SA-1B has over 1B masks from 11M licensed, privacy-preserving images. SAM and SA-1B are released, with SAM under the Apache 2.0 license. The text states that room for improvement remains, discussed in §8.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The paper builds a promptable segmentation task, the SAM model, and a data engine that produced SA-1B with over 1B masks.

sections.body: The task is to return a valid segmentation mask for any prompt, where a prompt can be foreground or background points, a rough box or mask, free-form text, or other information about what to segment. When a prompt is ambiguous, the output should be a reasonable mask for at least one candidate object. The task also serves as the pre-training objective, simulating prompt sequences and comparing predictions to ground truth. Downstream tasks are solved by engineering prompts; for example, a cat detector's box can prompt the model for cat instance segmentation. The authors contrast this with multi-task systems, where training and test tasks are the same. They say the task adapts to "many (though not all)" existing and new segmentation tasks.
sections.heading: Segment Anything Task
sections.headline: Promptable segmentation asks for a valid mask from any prompt, and the same task serves as pre-training and zero-shot transfer.

sections.body: SAM has an image encoder, a prompt encoder, and a mask decoder. The image encoder is a Vision Transformer pre-trained with MAE, run once per image so its embedding can be reused across prompts. Points and boxes are positional encodings summed with learned embeddings, text uses a CLIP text encoder, and masks are embedded with convolutions. The decoder modifies a Transformer decoder block and adds a dynamic mask prediction head. To handle ambiguity, SAM predicts 3 masks per prompt, backpropagates only the minimum loss over those masks, and gives each mask a predicted IoU score. Mask supervision combines focal loss and dice loss.
sections.heading: Segment Anything Model
sections.headline: SAM pairs a pre-trained image encoder with a fast prompt encoder and mask decoder that predicts 3 masks per prompt.

sections.body: Segmentation masks are not abundant online, so the authors built a data engine with three stages. In the assisted-manual stage, professional annotators clicked points with SAM's help; annotation time per mask fell from 34 to 14 seconds as the model improved, producing 4.3M masks from 120k images. In the semi-automatic stage, confident masks were detected automatically and annotators labeled the remaining objects, adding 5.9M masks from 180k images for a total of 10.2M. In the fully automatic stage, SAM was prompted with a 32×32 grid of points, with confident and stable masks selected and duplicates removed by non-maximal suppression, yielding 1.1B masks.
sections.heading: Segment Anything Data Engine
sections.headline: A three-stage data engine moves from annotator-assisted labeling to fully automatic mask generation over all 11M images.

sections.body: SA-1B has 11M images, with an average resolution of 3300×4950 pixels, released with the shortest side set to 1500 pixels, and 1.1B masks. Of these masks, 99.1% were generated fully automatically, and SA-1B includes only automatic masks. To estimate mask quality, professional annotators corrected automatic masks on 500 images, about 50k masks. The authors report that 94% of pairs have greater than 90% IoU and 97% have greater than 75% IoU, compared with prior inter-annotator consistency of 85-91% IoU. Compared with Open Images, SA-1B has 11× more images, 400× more masks, and 36× more masks per image.
sections.heading: Segment Anything Dataset
sections.headline: SA-1B contains 1.1B masks, 99.1% generated automatically, and 94% of sampled automatic masks exceed 90% intersection-over-union with corrected versions.

sections.body: The authors examine geographic and income representation in SA-1B and the fairness of SAM for people. Table 1 shows 36.2% of SA-1B images from Asia & Oceania and 49.8% from Europe, while Africa has 2.8%; every region has at least 28 million masks. Fairness was tested on MIAP for gender and age and a proprietary dataset for skin tone, using 1 and 3 random points. At 1 point, mIoU was 54.4 ±1.7 for feminine and 55.7 ±1.7 for masculine, and 62.9 ±6.7 for older. The authors find no significant difference across skin tones and state that biases may arise when SAM is used in larger systems.
sections.heading: Segment Anything RAI Analysis
sections.headline: SAM performs similarly across perceived gender and skin tone groups, while the older age group scores highest with a wide confidence interval.

sections.body: The paper tests zero-shot transfer on five tasks. For single foreground point prompts, mIoU is computed on 23 datasets, and annotators rate masks from 1 to 10. SAM is higher than RITM on 16 of 23 datasets, and an oracle that picks the best of 3 masks beats RITM on all datasets. Human ratings for SAM fall between 7 and 9. For edge detection on BSDS500, SAM has ODS .768 and R50 .928, against .788 and .923 for HED, which is also trained on BSDS500. For LVIS v1 object proposals, SAM reaches mask AR@1000 of 59.3 versus 63.0 for ViTDet-H, and it outperforms ViTDet-H on medium, large, and rare objects. Text-to-mask results are qualitative and described as a proof of concept.
sections.heading: Zero-Shot Transfer Experiments
sections.headline: With one point, SAM beats the strongest interactive baseline on 16 of 23 datasets and receives higher human quality ratings.

sections.body: The authors place SAM within the foundation model framing, noting that image segmentation is an inherently limited but important subset of computer vision. They contrast the role of self-supervision: SAM is initialized with MAE, but the vast majority of its capabilities come from large-scale supervised training enabled by the data engine. They discuss composition, with MCC using SAM for 3D reconstruction and SAM prompted by gaze points from a wearable device. Stated limitations include missing fine structures, hallucinating small disconnected components, and boundaries less crisp than zoom-in methods. Dedicated interactive methods are expected to outperform SAM with many points, the text-to-mask task is exploratory, and simple prompts for semantic and panoptic segmentation are unclear.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors argue SAM's capabilities come mostly from supervised training, and list missed fine structures and limited text-to-mask reliability as limits.

sections.body: The appendix covers SAM and task details, automatic mask generation, additional RAI details, experiment implementation, the human study design, dataset, annotation, and model cards, and annotation guidelines. It specifies a ViT-H/16 image encoder with 1024×1024 input, a two-layer mask decoder, and a training recipe of 90k iterations with batch size 256. Automatic mask generation uses a 32×32 grid on the full image plus 20 zoomed-in crops. The model card reports training on 256 A100 GPUs for 68 hours, an estimated 6963 kWh, and an estimated 2.8 metric tons of carbon dioxide.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists architecture, training, automatic mask generation, fairness, study design, model and dataset cards, and annotation guidelines.
